title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models

paper.title: A Scaled-Up Empirical Study of Syntactic Language Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored.
We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations—one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks—at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks.
The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention.
We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Standard causal language models process text as flat token sequences. Although they can learn distributional proxies for syntax Hu et al. (2020) , hierarchical constituency structures—phrases composing into sentences—are left implicit. Syntactic language models (SLMs) inject syntactic biases into Transformers Vaswani et al. (2017) . One approach jointly models surface sentences and linearized versions of their syntactic parse trees Sartran et al. (2022) ; Zhao et al. (2024) . These models typically employ structural attention masks that allow a non-terminal to compose its child tokens once they are generated by focusing its attention on them. Zhao et al. (2025) conduct a systematic empirical comparison of various design choices for SLMs, but they do not fully explore the complete design space of tree linearization and attention masks. Moreover, prior SLM studies have mostly evaluated models up to 300M parameters, trained on up to 9B tokens, and tested on only two or three tasks. In this paper, we conduct a larger-scale empirical study of SLMs, evaluating selected models with up to 1B parameters and approximately 100B terminal training tokens on 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. We investigate a design space of 12 configurations: one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants with different tree linearizations and attention masks. Our BBC experiments cover the full family at 100M and eight configurations at 500M on deduplicated data, with pause-token controls in both settings. We then study causal tree models and pause-token baselines at 1B on FineWeb-Edu. Our findings are as follows: (i) Tree linearization with standard causal attention provides strong generation and syntactic performance. In both BBC settings, Tree and TGTree outperform structural-mask variants on XSum; TGTree also achieves the highest BLiMP score at 500M. Hybrid attention improves document perplexity, showing that the preferred attention mechanism depends on the objective. (ii) At 1B on FineWeb-Edu, TGTree and Pause-2 have similar average downstream accuracy, while tree models perform better on syntactic evaluation. Explicit structure thus remains useful, but its benefits must be assessed against the additional computation introduced by structural tokens. Our contributions are: • We scale SLM evaluation to 1B parameters and approximately 100B terminal training tokens, across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. • We systematically examine tree linearization and attention design on BBC News at 100M and deduplicated BBC News at 500M. • We compare SLMs with pause-token baselines to assess the benefits of explicit structure alongside additional token positions.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Prior work on syntactic language models (SLMs) has explored a broad range of ways to incorporate linguistic structure into neural sequence modeling. Transformer Grammars (TG) Sartran et al. (2022) encode constituency trees as a sequence of actions and enforce hierarchical attention patterns. A subsequent study extends the idea to dependency trees Zhao et al. (2024) . Building on this line of work, Zhao et al. (2025) provide the most systematic comparison of SLM design choices including those of tree linearization and composition mechanisms. These studies show that syntactic inductive bias can improve language modeling and syntactic evaluation, but they typically couple modeling of linearized trees with specialized attention mechanisms. Other studies incorporate syntactic inductive bias through alternative architectural mechanisms rather than explicit representations. These approaches include latent structure induction during pretraining Hu et al. (2024) , stack-based recursive state tracking Murty et al. (2023) , and dependency-graph-informed attention mechanisms Huang et al. (2026) .

sections.heading: 3.1 Syntactic Language Models
sections.text: Let 𝐱 = ( x 1 , … , x N ) \mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}) be a sentence of N N terminal tokens, and let 𝐲 \mathbf{y} be a labeled constituency parse tree for 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , where each node carries a phrase category (e.g., S , NP , or VP ) and spans a contiguous subsequence of 𝐱 \mathbf{x} . A syntactic language model predicts the sentence and its structural representation through a linearized token sequence 𝐳 = ( z 1 , … , z T ) \mathbf{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{T}) , factorized autoregressively as p ⁡ ( 𝐳 := Linearize ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) ) = ∏ t = 1 T p ⁡ ( z t ∣ z < t ) p(\mathbf{z}:=\textsc{Linearize}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}))=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p(z_{t}\mid z_{<t}) (1) where Linearize maps the sentence–tree pair into a flat sequence. When the mapping is one-to-one, p ⁡ ( 𝐳 ) p(\mathbf{z}) is the joint probability p ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) ; lossy linearizations can assign the same sequence to multiple trees. Prior SLMs vary in the linearization that serializes the tree 𝐲 \mathbf{y} into 𝐳 \mathbf{z} , and the architecture that parameterizes the conditional probabilities p ⁡ ( z t ∣ z < t ) p(z_{t}\mid z_{<t}) . In Transformer-based SLMs, this architectural choice is largely realized through the attention mechanism , which governs how syntactic relationships among tokens in 𝐳 \mathbf{z} are processed.

sections.heading: 3.3 Structural Attention
sections.text: A Transformer-based SLM can also incorporate structural information directly into the model itself via specially-designed attention mechanisms. We study three attention mechanisms as listed below.

sections.heading: Causal Attention
sections.text: The joint p ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) is modeled through standard autoregressive factorization over 𝐳 = Linearize ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) \mathbf{z}=\textsc{Linearize}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) with no modification to the attention mechanism. Constituency structures are encoded entirely in the token sequence; the model learns to route information through Opening Non-Terminal (ONT) and Closing Non-Terminal (CNT) using standard causal attention.

sections.heading: Structural Attention
sections.text: Structural attention factorizes p ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) autoregressively over the linearized tree sequence z = Lin 2 ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) z=\textsc{Lin}^{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) and uses structure-dependent masks. In the original Transformer Grammar (TG) formulation Sartran et al. (2022) , each CNT is duplicated into two actions. CNT 1 performs COMPOSE attention over only the current constituent’s children, producing a composed representation. CNT 2 performs STACK attention over only the representations on the active parse stack. TG then hides the child representations from later positions, forcing them to access the constituent through CNT 1 . Zhao et al. (2025) isolate this post-composition masking and show that removing it yields consistently better performance. We call the resulting variant Nomask : it retains the COMPOSE mask at CNT 1 but gives all other positions causal access to earlier terminals, ONTs, and CNT 1 representations. Thus, “no mask” refers specifically to removing TG’s post-composition mask, not to unrestricted bidirectional attention. Our default Nomask still hides CNT 2 states from later positions; Nomask-Aug exposes them as well.

sections.heading: Hybrid Attention
sections.text: The hybrid attention mechanism factorizes p ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) p(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) autoregressively over z = Lin 2 ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) z=\textsc{Lin}^{2}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}) and replaces standard causal attention with head-level mask mixing : rather than applying a single mask type across all attention heads, different heads receive different masks. Hybrid attention enables the model to combine multiple structural attention patterns within a single Transformer layer. Since enumerating all possible head-level mask assignments is computationally infeasible, we restrict ourselves to a straightforward setting: half of the attention heads receive one type of structural mask, and the remaining heads use another (either causal or structural). This configuration provides a tractable way to study hybrid attention. Table 3 summarizes the 12 controlled configurations across the tree-linearization and attention-mask designs studied in our framework.

sections.heading: 4 Terminal Format Evaluation
sections.text: To evaluate SLMs on multiple-choice (MC) tasks, we follow the OLMES completion/cloze formulation Gu et al. (2025) with multi-shot in-context demonstrations. Each answer is treated as a candidate completion, rather than as a label predicted from a displayed option list. We parse both the context and continuation with Benepar Kitaev and Klein (2018) and use their respective 1-best constituency parses. Appendix B.5 provides the complete input construction. SLM continuations interleave terminal content with structural ONT and CNT tokens, creating a choice between scoring the complete sequence and scoring only terminal tokens. Let 𝐩 \mathbf{p} denote the evaluation context and 𝐜 j \mathbf{c}_{j} the linearized continuation for candidate j j . Let 𝒯 ⁡ ( 𝐜 j ) \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{c}_{j}) and 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐜 j ) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{c}_{j}) denote its terminal and non-terminal indices, respectively. For prediction, we apply the task-specific normalization to S term S_{\mathrm{term}} : tasks using length normalization divide by the terminal continuation’s character count, and the remaining tasks use the raw sum. The candidate with the highest resulting score is selected. Appendix F compares the two raw scores on an eight-task suite and describes its overlap with the main evaluation.

sections.heading: 5.1 Setup
sections.text: We train models from scratch for one epoch over each run’s training stream using the same OLMo-based Groeneveld et al. (2024) decoder-only Transformer family. Learning rates and batch sizes follow the Step Law Li et al. (2025) using each representation’s actual training token budget. Causal models use FlashAttention-2 Dao (2024) , while structural and hybrid models use specialized attention kernels. Appendix A provides the architectures and training hyperparameters. sections.heading: 5.3 Experiment 1: Disentangling Tree Linearization and Attention
sections.text: We study two BBC News training settings, using articles from FineWeb Penedo et al. (2024) and constituency parses from Benepar Kitaev and Klein (2018) . The deduplicated reference corpus contains 1.47M articles and 0.801B terminal tokens (Table 2 ). At 100M, we evaluate all 12 controlled configurations, two pause-token controls, and Pushdown on the original stream, including repeated and near-duplicate articles. At 500M, we evaluate eight configurations and two pause-token controls on the deduplicated version. Table 4 reports both experiments. We compare variants within each setting; differences in article versions, cumulative training exposure, and optimization prevent attributing cross-setting changes to model scale alone. The dedup runs use reserved-clean development and test sets of 1,000 and 5,000 documents. We evaluate Doc-PPL for both settings on this same test set, replacing the earlier PPL split after identifying substantial training overlap. Appendix D describes the data audit and additional 500M experiments on the original corpus.

sections.heading: Structural Attention vs. Causal Attention.
sections.text: Tree and TGTree achieve the highest XSum means in both BBC settings. At 100M, they exceed TGNomask-Aug and TG, whereas TGNomask-Aug has the highest BLiMP score. At dedup 500M, Tree and TGTree exceed TGNomask by more than 1.4 XSum points and TG by more than 2.8 points; TGTree also leads on BLiMP. Removing TG’s post-composition mask improves XSum, BoolQ, and perplexity in both settings, consistent with Zhao et al. (2025) . Causal attention does not lead on every task: TGNomask exceeds TGTree on SG and BoolQ at 500M, and Terminal has the highest BoolQ mean in that setting.

sections.heading: Hybrid Attention.
sections.text: Mixing causal and structural heads improves TGTree’s document perplexity from 14.709 to 14.482 at 100M and from 13.947 to 13.785 at dedup 500M, giving the lowest value in each setting. At 500M, it also improves BoolQ by 0.98 points, but lowers XSum, SG, and BLiMP. Mixing TGNomask and TG heads likewise lowers perplexity in both settings. Hybrid attention is therefore useful for language modeling, even though it does not improve on causal Tree models for summarization.

sections.heading: Pause-token Controls.
sections.text: Pause tokens improve XSum over Terminal in both settings, indicating that additional token positions can help generation. Tree and TGTree nevertheless exceed their corresponding pause controls on XSum, SG, BLiMP, and document perplexity. At 500M, both tree models gain more than 11 BLiMP points. Both linearizations have higher perplexity than Tree in their respective settings. The lowest perplexity comes from hybrid attention, whereas the highest XSum mean comes from TGTree. sections.heading: Tree Linearization Ablations.
sections.text: Removing opening non-terminals improves SG but lowers XSum in both settings, suggesting that opening tokens are more useful for generation than for the distinctions tested by SG. Doubling closing tokens gives the highest XSum mean in both experiments. At 100M, tripling them further improves SG and BLiMP over TGTree but lowers XSum; merging consecutive closing tokens lowers SG. Shuffling structural tokens causes a substantial BLiMP decline. The SG subtask results for dedup 500M appear in Appendix E .

sections.heading: Scaling Up.
sections.text: We study Tree and TGTree at 1B because of their generation performance and compatibility with efficient causal attention. They use the same attention architecture as Terminal and the pause-token baselines, enabling a direct comparison of input representations. Appendix A.2 reports throughput measurements for the earlier implementations.

sections.heading: 5.4 Experiment 2: Scaling to 1B on FineWeb-Edu
sections.text: FineWeb-Edu-100BT Penedo et al. (2024) is a ∼ \sim 100B-token sampled subset of the FineWeb-Edu corpus, filtered for educational quality and spanning diverse domains. We train five models at 1B parameters on this data: Terminal, Tree, TGTree, Pause-1 and Pause-2. Evaluation uses the 11-task OLMES suite Gu et al. (2025) , with the content-focused terminal score as the primary MC metric (§ 4 ), together with the SG and BLiMP syntactic benchmarks. Table 5 reports per-task downstream accuracy, and Table 6 reports the syntactic evaluation results. We quantify evaluation-set uncertainty using 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples; full confidence intervals and tests appear in Appendix C , and Appendix F reports sensitivity to full versus terminal scoring.

sections.heading: Downstream Performance.
sections.text: TGTree achieves the highest average accuracy across the 11 tasks (55.88), exceeding Terminal by 2.68 points. Its gains over Terminal are significant on five tasks under paired bootstrap tests. Tree improves the average by only 0.36 points and performs particularly poorly on HellaSwag, suggesting that the choice of linearization remains important at this scale.

sections.heading: Explicit Structure vs.  Dummy Tokens.
sections.text: TGTree and Pause-2 have nearly identical average accuracy (55.88 vs. 55.80), with complementary strengths. TGTree is significantly better on BoolQ, while Pause-2 is significantly better on HellaSwag; differences on the other nine tasks are not significant at α = .05 \alpha=.05 . Excluding BoolQ puts Pause-2 ahead (55.04 vs. 54.71). These results show that a strong non-structural baseline can achieve similar aggregate downstream accuracy to an SLM under approximately comparable token budgets. Appendix C reports the paired comparisons, and Appendix F.1 examines an alternative task suite. sections.heading: Syntactic Evaluation.
sections.text: Tree achieves the highest scores on both syntactic benchmarks, exceeding Terminal by 2.14 points on BLiMP and 1.94 points on SG (Table 6 ). TGTree also improves both scores. Pause tokens improve BLiMP but lower SG relative to Terminal, leaving a larger gap to the tree models on this benchmark. Thus, the similar downstream averages of TGTree and Pause-2 coexist with a syntactic advantage for explicit tree representations.

sections.heading: 6.1 Why Does Tree Linearization Help Without Structural Attention?
sections.text: We propose three complementary hypotheses:

sections.heading: Implicit multi-task learning hypothesis.
sections.text: The model jointly predicts terminal tokens and syntactic structure, making constituency boundaries explicit through non-terminals instead of inferring them only from co-occurrence statistics. Sartran et al. (2022) attribute the perplexity gains of such joint modeling to the “additional syntactic supervision” that non-terminals provide by constraining admissible word classes at each position.

sections.heading: Compositional bottleneck hypothesis.
sections.text: CNT positions may act as “summary points” that encourage compression of constituent information. Under this hypothesis, causal attention allows the model to learn which information to route through CNT positions, unlike TG’s hard-coded COMPOSE attention. It can also preserve direct access to earlier words when a task requires lexical detail. We do not directly test this mechanism.

sections.heading: Adaptive computation hypothesis.
sections.text: Pause- K K allocates a fixed number of learned latent tokens after each terminal. Tree models instead use parse-dependent structural tokens: richer constituency structures introduce more ONT/CNT positions at phrase boundaries. This placement may allocate additional computation near constituent composition. The gains of both tree and pause-token models over Terminal motivate studying how the number and placement of these positions affect learning.

sections.heading: 6.2 Syntactic Generalization and Downstream Performance
sections.text: The best linearization differs between syntactic evaluation and downstream tasks. In both BBC settings, Tree-NoONT has the highest SG score, whereas TGTree has the highest XSum mean. On FineWeb-Edu, Tree leads on both syntactic benchmarks, but TGTree has the higher downstream average. Predicting additional structural tokens therefore does not improve all forms of syntactic generalization equally. The pause-token comparisons further distinguish these outcomes. Pause-2 approaches TGTree’s average downstream accuracy at 1B, yet remains below it on SG and BLiMP. Additional token positions can support downstream performance without producing the same syntactic behavior as explicit tree tokens. This distinction motivates evaluating SLMs on both targeted syntactic tests and a broad downstream suite.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We conduct a scaled-up empirical study of syntactic language models, examining tree linearization and attention design and evaluating selected models up to 1B parameters. Across BBC 100M and dedup 500M, causal tree models achieve strong generation and syntactic performance while remaining compatible with FlashAttention; hybrid attention provides the best document perplexity. At 1B on FineWeb-Edu, TGTree and Pause-2 have similar aggregate downstream performance, while tree models retain an advantage on syntactic evaluation. These findings support tree linearization as a practical way to introduce syntactic bias and highlight the need to compare its benefits with those of additional non-structural computation.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Constructing linearized tree inputs requires a parser for training and evaluation. This adds preprocessing cost, and parsing errors may propagate into the model. We do not quantify the effect of parse quality and study only English. The compositional bottleneck and adaptive computation accounts remain hypotheses; testing them would require interventions on the models’ internal representations or attention patterns. Each pretraining configuration is represented by one run. The five BBC seeds capture fine-tuning variation, while the FineWeb-Edu bootstrap intervals capture evaluation uncertainty. Neither measures variation across pretraining runs. BBC rankings are descriptive, and the FineWeb-Edu per-task tests are exploratory without multiple-comparison correction. The historical BBC PPL test contains substantial training overlap. Our replacement splits were filtered against the historical corpus. A full token-level audit finds no exact document matches against the deduplicated training arrays; normalized-text, near-duplicate, and local-fragment checks against those arrays remain incomplete. The BBC and FineWeb-Edu experiments differ in data, token budgets, and optimization settings, so they do not isolate the effects of deduplication or scale. Pause-token controls approximately match sequence lengths rather than exact FLOPs. We do not evaluate structural-mask models at 1B on FineWeb-Edu. Document PPL approximates the parse marginal using a finite candidate set and one selected history. The multiple-choice evaluation conditions on silver parses and omits structural-token likelihoods; its scoring analysis reuses several main-evaluation splits. Public code, configurations, and selected result evidence are available, while full data and checkpoint downloads remain pending.

sections.heading: Data Preparation.
sections.text: The deduplicated BBC reference corpus contains 1,466,132 articles from 89 crawl shards spanning 2013–2022. We remove exact terminal-sequence, normalized-text, and near-duplicate articles from the historical parsed crawl pool, then encode retained articles with PTB mapping and explicit BOS/EOS tokens. The terminal representation contains 800,848,405 tokens (0.801B); tree representations add the structural tokens listed in Table 8 . We evaluate the final checkpoint from each run. Training loss includes structural or pause targets, whereas document PPL is normalized by terminal and EOS tokens. Data manifests, tokenizer definitions, and checkpoint identifiers are provided with the code.

Table 9 reports throughput from the earlier H800 implementation, where structural models used FlexAttention Dong et al. (2025) . These measurements describe that implementation; throughput was not remeasured under a common setup for the RTX 5090 runs. Earlier campaign summaries report 133 hours on four H800 GPUs for the 100M variants, 125 hours on four H800 GPUs for the historical 500M campaign, and 385 hours on 64 A800 GPUs for the 1B variants. sections.heading: A.3 Tokenizer and Structural Tokens
sections.text: We use tokenizers with reserved non-terminal tokens (e.g., NP) , (S , and VP) ). The tokenizer is based on the GPT-2 tokenizer Radford et al. (2019) or the Qwen3 tokenizer Yang et al. (2025) . For tree linearization models, opening non-terminals (ONT) and closing non-terminals (CNT) are represented as reserved tokens so that linearized constituency structure is preserved during pretraining and evaluation.

sections.heading: B.1 Downstream Fine-Tuning on BBC News: XSum and BoolQ
sections.text: On BBC News, we evaluate XSum and BoolQ through task-specific fine-tuning from each pretrained checkpoint, with the optimizer state reset. We use the full XSum test set (11,333 examples) and BoolQ validation set (3,270 questions). All models are fine-tuned with AdamW ( β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}{=}0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}{=}0.95 , weight decay 0.1) and a cosine learning rate schedule with 100 warmup steps decaying to 10 − 6 10^{-6} .

sections.heading: XSum.
sections.text: We fine-tune all models for 3 epochs with a peak learning rate of 6 × 10 − 5 6\times 10^{-5} and a global batch size of 40. During evaluation, we generate summaries with beam search using a beam size of 6 and a maximum length of 150 tokens. For tree linearization models, beam search proceeds at the word level (word-sync) with a maximum of 75 word steps and a grammar constraint of at most 4 consecutive opening non-terminals. ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2, and ROUGE-L are computed with the standard evaluate library; R-AVG denotes their arithmetic mean.

sections.heading: BoolQ.
sections.text: We fine-tune all models for 5 epochs with peak LR 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , global batch size 40. We measure accuracy on the validation split. The XSum and BoolQ entries in Tables 4 and 12 are means ± \pm sample standard deviations over five fine-tuning seeds (42, 2026, 6198, 13171, and 31723). Pushdown uses right-binarized, unary-collapsed silver spans. Its XSum decoder conditions on the source parse and jointly searches summary tokens and attachment actions with beam size 6 and no limit on consecutive reductions. BoolQ uses teacher-forced candidate scoring with supplied parser spans.

The logarithm base does not affect the SG predictions because the task-specific formulas only compare surprisals. sections.heading: B.3 BLiMP
sections.text: BLiMP Warstadt et al. (2020) evaluates whether models assign higher likelihood to grammatical sentences in minimal pairs across 12 grammatical phenomena. For tree-linearization models, we obtain 300 parse proposals ( K = 300 K=300 ) from the Benepar parser Kitaev and Klein (2018) and score each sentence by summing the joint probabilities of its candidate sequences. Tree-NoONT and Tree-Compress BLiMP scores have not been reevaluated with sequence deduplication; their reported values are marked accordingly. A pair is scored correct if the good sentence receives higher marginalized probability than the bad sentence. Each of the 67 subtasks contains 1,000 pairs. For terminal and pause-token models, K = 1 K=1 (no tree marginalization). Tree-Shuffle likewise uses terminal-format scoring with K = 1 K=1 . Pushdown’s supplied-tree scorer sums token likelihoods conditioned on candidate attachment sequences, without attachment probabilities. Its historical BLiMP result is retained as a reference; the exact scoring snapshot for that run is unavailable, so we do not interpret it as joint token–attachment marginalization.

sections.heading: B.4 Model-Specific Document-PPL Protocols
sections.text: For reserved-clean-v1, all 5,000 documents, 129,085 sentences, and 3,068,713 terminal/EOS tokens are scored. The base terminal array contains 3,073,713 positions; one BOS per document is context only. For Tree/TG candidates, 122,338 sentences have 300 unique valid candidates and 6,747 have 122. Repeated padding slots are excluded from Eq. 6 . Candidate joint likelihoods follow each model’s label mask, with no parser weighting or division by candidate count. After scoring the candidates for each sentence, we retain the highest-probability sequence as context for the next sentence, breaking ties by candidate order. Histories reset at document boundaries, and padding positions are excluded from the retained cache. Evaluation uses FP32 with SDPA and disables TF32. Candidate microbatches share the sentence’s padding length. Tree-NoONT and Tree-Compress can map different proposal trees to the same token sequence. NoONT removes opening tokens, while Compress merges consecutive closing tokens and discards their number and labels. We deduplicate the complete, unpadded sequences within each sentence after applying these transformations, retaining the first occurrence. Each distinct sequence contributes once to Eq. 6 , irrespective of how many proposal trees map to it. We reevaluate NoONT at 100M and dedup 500M and Compress at 100M under this rule. The full test contains 37,524,534 valid original proposals. NoONT has repeated projected sequences in 117,847 sentences, leaving 34,053,187 distinct candidates; Compress has repeats in 57,733 sentences, leaving 37,177,859. All candidate terminal projections and document boundaries are checked against the same test corpus. Their BLiMP candidates still need the corresponding check; we retain the recorded scores with markers and exclude them from claims about marginalized likelihood. Tree-Shuffle uses the masked historical checkpoint with terminal-only scoring. Pushdown uses native n-ary attachment candidates, the v1 stack-legal action space, joint token–attachment sums, and model-best histories. These two models use distinct probability/candidate spaces and are contextual comparisons, not entries in the controlled Tree/TG PPL ranking. Neither is included in the new ten-model experiment. The BBC 100M models in Table 4 and historical 500M checkpoints in Appendix D use the same reserved-clean PPL protocol. TripleCNT is evaluated with its corresponding grammar. The earlier PPL values, which used the overlapping test and parser-first histories, are excluded.

sections.heading: B.5 OLMES Multiple-Choice Evaluation on FineWeb-Edu
sections.text: All 11 downstream tasks use the completion/cloze formulation standardized in OLMES Gu et al. (2025) . This formulation evaluates each answer string separately as a natural-language completion instead of predicting an answer label. All evaluations are multi-shot. We use 5-shot prompts for HellaSwag, WinoGrande, MMLU, MMLU-Redux, and OpenBookQA, and 3-shot prompts for BoolQ, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, PIQA, SocialIQA, and CommonsenseQA. We preprocess the natural-language content of every demonstration, target prompt, and answer option with Benepar Kitaev and Klein (2018) . For each parsed component x x , we retain only its 1-best constituency parse 𝐲 ^ ​ ( x ) \hat{\mathbf{y}}(x) as a silver tree. Depending on the task template, fields are parsed separately or the completed candidate sequence is parsed and split at the cloze boundary. Task-specific template text is represented with the same constituency-tree notation. The resulting trees are converted to the linearization required by each model. Thus, the syntactic inputs differ in representation but share the same underlying terminal prompt and answer text. For each demonstration, the parsed gold answer suffix is appended to its parsed prompt. These demonstrations precede the target instance in every candidate prefix 𝐩 j \mathbf{p}_{j} . We then append the candidate-specific parsed suffix 𝐜 j \mathbf{c}_{j} and score only that suffix conditional on 𝐩 j \mathbf{p}_{j} . The prediction is arg ⁡ max j ⁡ S ⁡ ( 𝐜 j ∣ 𝐩 j ) \arg\max_{j}S(\mathbf{c}_{j}\mid\mathbf{p}_{j}) , using the task-specific option-score normalization. The primary results use S term S_{\text{term}} in Eq. 5 ; Appendix F also reports S full S_{\text{full}} . For WinoGrande, the answer fills the blank in a candidate-specific prefix, while the common post-blank text is the scored suffix, following OLMES. Unlike BLiMP, this MC protocol uses one silver tree per textual component and uses neither multiple parse proposals nor tree marginalization.

Affiliation: School of Information Science and Technology, ShanghaiTech University Affiliation: Shanghai Engineering Research Center of Intelligent Vision and Imaging Email: louchaobrn@outlook.com Abstract Syntactic language models (SLMs) that generate sentences along with their syntactic tree structures have shown promise in both syntactic generalization and downstream tasks. Prior studies, however, have mostly evaluated smaller models trained on less pretraining data and tested on narrower task suites. In addition, the design space of tree linearization and attention masks remains underexplored. We conduct a large-scale empirical study of 12 controlled configurations—one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants spanning different linearizations and masks—at scales up to 1B parameters and 100B training tokens, evaluated across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. The experimental results show that SLMs with standard causal attention match or exceed structural-mask variants across downstream and syntactic benchmarks. They require no architectural modifications and remain compatible with FlashAttention. We also observe that when scaling up to the 1B-parameter scale, the top-performing SLM variant no longer shows a clear advantage over a compute-matched non-structural baseline, suggesting that SLMs may become less competitive with scale. Our code is available at https://github.com/qlwpc/TG-Interpolation . 1 Introduction Standard causal language models process text as flat token sequences. Although they can learn distributional proxies for syntax Hu et al. (2020) , hierarchical constituency structures—phrases composing into sentences—are left implicit. Syntactic language models (SLMs) inject syntactic biases into Transformers Vaswani et al. (2017) . One approach jointly models surface sentences and linearized versions of their syntactic parse trees Sartran et al. (2022) ; Zhao et al. (2024) . These models typically employ structural attention masks that allow a non-terminal to compose its child tokens once they are generated by focusing its attention on them. Zhao et al. (2025) conduct a systematic empirical comparison of various design choices for SLMs, but they do not fully explore the complete design space of tree linearization and attention masks. Moreover, prior SLM studies have mostly evaluated models up to 300M parameters, trained on up to 9B tokens, and tested on only two or three tasks. In this paper, we conduct a larger-scale empirical study of SLMs, evaluating selected models with up to 1B parameters and approximately 100B terminal training tokens on 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. We investigate a design space of 12 configurations: one terminal baseline and 11 SLM variants with different tree linearizations and attention masks. Our BBC experiments cover the full family at 100M and eight configurations at 500M on deduplicated data, with pause-token controls in both settings. We then study causal tree models and pause-token baselines at 1B on FineWeb-Edu. Our findings are as follows: (i) Tree linearization with standard causal attention provides strong generation and syntactic performance. In both BBC settings, Tree and TGTree outperform structural-mask variants on XSum; TGTree also achieves the highest BLiMP score at 500M. Hybrid attention improves document perplexity, showing that the preferred attention mechanism depends on the objective. (ii) At 1B on FineWeb-Edu, TGTree and Pause-2 have similar average downstream accuracy, while tree models perform better on syntactic evaluation. Explicit structure thus remains useful, but its benefits must be assessed against the additional computation introduced by structural tokens. Our contributions are: • We scale SLM evaluation to 1B parameters and approximately 100B terminal training tokens, across 11 downstream tasks and two syntactic benchmarks. • We systematically examine tree linearization and attention design on BBC News at 100M and deduplicated BBC News at 500M. • We compare SLMs with pause-token baselines to assess the benefits of explicit structure alongside additional token positions. 2 Related Work Prior work on syntactic language models (SLMs) has explored a broad range of ways to incorporate linguistic structure into neural sequence modeling. Transformer Grammars (TG) Sartran et al. (2022) encode constituency trees as a sequence of actions and enforce hierarchical attention patterns. A subsequent study extends the idea to dependency trees Zhao et al. (2024) . Building on this line of work, Zhao et al. (2025) provide the most systematic comparison of SLM design choices including those of tree linearization and composition mechanisms. These studies show that syntactic inductive bias can improve language modeling and syntactic evaluation, but they typically couple modeling of linearized trees with specialized attention mechanisms. Other studies incorporate syntactic inductive bias through alternative architectural mechanisms rather than explicit representations. These approaches include latent structure induction during pretraining Hu et al. (2024) , stack-based recursive state tracking Murty et al. (2023) , and dependency-graph-informed attention mechanisms Huang et al. (2026) . 3 Variants of Syntactic Language Models 3.1 Syntactic Language Models Let 𝐱 = ( x 1 , … , x N ) \mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}) be a sentence of N N terminal tokens, and let 𝐲 \mathbf{y} be a labeled constituency parse tree for 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , where each node carries a phrase category (e.g., S , NP , or VP ) and spans a contiguous subsequence of 𝐱 \mathbf{x} . In the original Transformer Grammar (TG) formulation Sartran et al. (2022) , each CNT is duplicated into two actions. CNT 1 performs COMPOSE attention over only the current constituent’s children, producing a composed representation. CNT 2 performs STACK attention over only the representations on the active parse stack. TG then hides the child representations from later positions, forcing them to access the constituent through CNT 1 . Zhao et al. (2025) isolate this post-composition masking and show that removing it yields consistently better performance. We call the resulting variant Nomask : it retains the COMPOSE mask at CNT 1 but gives all other positions causal access to earlier terminals, ONTs, and CNT 1 representations. Thus, “no mask” refers specifically to removing TG’s post-composition mask, not to unrestricted bidirectional attention. Our default Nomask still hides CNT 2 states from later positions; Nomask-Aug exposes them as well. Hybrid attention enables the model to combine multiple structural attention patterns within a single Transformer layer. Since enumerating all possible head-level mask assignments is computationally infeasible, we restrict ourselves to a straightforward setting: half of the attention heads receive one type of structural mask, and the remaining heads use another (either causal or structural). This configuration provides a tractable way to study hybrid attention. We propose three complementary hypotheses: Implicit multi-task learning hypothesis. The model jointly predicts terminal tokens and syntactic structure, making constituency boundaries explicit through non-terminals instead of inferring them only from co-occurrence statistics. Sartran et al. (2022) attribute the perplexity gains of such joint modeling to the “additional syntactic supervision” that non-terminals provide by constraining admissible word classes at each position. Compositional bottleneck hypothesis. CNT positions may act as “summary points” that encourage compression of constituent information. Under this hypothesis, causal attention allows the model to learn which information to route through CNT positions, unlike TG’s hard-coded COMPOSE attention. It can also preserve direct access to earlier words when a task requires lexical detail. We do not directly test this mechanism. Adaptive computation hypothesis. Pause- K K allocates a fixed number of learned latent tokens after each terminal. Tree models instead use parse-dependent structural tokens: richer constituency structures introduce more ONT/CNT positions at phrase boundaries. This placement may allocate additional computation near constituent composition. The gains of both tree and pause-token models over Terminal motivate studying how the number and placement of these positions affect learning. 6.2 Syntactic Generalization and Downstream Performance The best linearization differs between syntactic evaluation and downstream tasks. In both BBC settings, Tree-NoONT has the highest SG score, whereas TGTree has the highest XSum mean. On FineWeb-Edu, Tree leads on both syntactic benchmarks, but TGTree has the higher downstream average. Predicting additional structural tokens therefore does not improve all forms of syntactic generalization equally. The pause-token comparisons further distinguish these outcomes. Pause-2 approaches TGTree’s average downstream accuracy at 1B, yet remains below it on SG and BLiMP. Additional token positions can support downstream performance without producing the same syntactic behavior as explicit tree tokens. This distinction motivates evaluating SLMs on both targeted syntactic tests and a broad downstream suite. 7 Conclusion We conduct a scaled-up empirical study of syntactic language models, examining tree linearization and attention design and evaluating selected models up to 1B parameters. Across BBC 100M and dedup 500M, causal tree models achieve strong generation and syntactic performance while remaining compatible with FlashAttention; hybrid attention provides the best document perplexity. At 1B on FineWeb-Edu, TGTree and Pause-2 have similar aggregate downstream performance, while tree models retain an advantage on syntactic evaluation. These findings support tree linearization as a practical way to introduce syntactic bias and highlight the need to compare its benefits with those of additional non-structural computation. Limitations Constructing linearized tree inputs requires a parser for training and evaluation. This adds preprocessing cost, and parsing errors may propagate into the model. We do not quantify the effect of parse quality and study only English. The compositional bottleneck and adaptive computation accounts remain hypotheses; testing them would require interventions on the models’ internal representations or attention patterns. Each pretraining configuration is represented by one run. The five BBC seeds capture fine-tuning variation, while the FineWeb-Edu bootstrap intervals capture evaluation uncertainty. Neither measures variation across pretraining runs. BBC rankings are descriptive, and the FineWeb-Edu per-task tests are exploratory without multiple-comparison correction. The historical BBC PPL test contains substantial training overlap. Our replacement splits were filtered against the historical corpus. A full token-level audit finds no exact document matches against the deduplicated training arrays; normalized-text, near-duplicate, and local-fragment checks against those arrays remain incomplete. The BBC and FineWeb-Edu experiments differ in data, token budgets, and optimization settings, so they do not isolate the effects of deduplication or scale. Pause-token controls approximately match sequence lengths rather than exact FLOPs. We do not evaluate structural-mask models at 1B on FineWeb-Edu. Document PPL approximates the parse marginal using a finite candidate set and one selected history. The multiple-choice evaluation conditions on silver parses and omits structural-token likelihoods; its scoring analysis reuses several main-evaluation splits. Public code, configurations, and selected result evidence are available, while full data and checkpoint downloads remain pending.
